newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan tycoon announces US$400 bln venture capital.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan tycoon announces US$400 bln venture capital.

text.p: Taiwan tycoon Jeffrey Koo on Monday announced the formation of a venture capital firm with US$400 million in private funds for investment in Asia-Pacific companies.

Koo, chairman of Chinatrust Commercial Bank, has long been keen to pioneer investment banking in Taiwan, and he said the newly formed Crimson Asia Capital Holdings Ltd was a major step towards that goal.
"This fund aims to expand Taiwan's service in the investment banking sector because that is an area where Taiwan lags behind foreign banks," Koo told a news conference announcing the project.
"This is a necessary step in the internationalisation of Taiwan's banks." he said.

The firm, with US$400 million of initial capital pooled from Koo's own family fortune and private interests in the Middle East, Europe, Asia and the United States, began operation on July 1 and would complete all investments in five years, Koo said.
"After the five-year period we will then raise more funds for second- and third-stage investments," Koo said.
Koo's son, Chinatrust senior vice president Jeffrey Koo Jr, will run Crimson's daily operations as executive director.
Chinatrust, one of Taiwan's most ambitious private banks, had said in 1996 that it planned to pioneer investment banking in Taiwan.
But Koo said Chinatrust did not take a stake in Crimson, which is registered in the Cayman Islands.
Initial investment into the fund already has been secured from four regions -- the Middle East, Europe, the United States and Asia -- each with a roughly one-quarter stake, Koo said.
The Koo family itself holds 10 percent, he said.
Koo declined to identify other investors.
The fund was expected to generate an investment return of 30 percent, Koo said.
Koo gave some details of how the funds would be invested, saying 25-30 percent would be poured into Taiwan itself.
The rest would divided among various Asian countries, mainly the Philippines, Japan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
Ten percent would be earmarked for investment in listed shares, while the rest would be invested in promising unlisted firms, Koo said.
Ten percent of the capital will be steered toward real estate investments, he added.
